newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Malaysia now key to Fokker rescue.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia now key to Fokker rescue.

text.p: Bankrupt Dutch planemaker Fokker NV said Thursday that Dutch parties involved in possible rescue talks had agreed on a relaunch with the financial aid of the Malaysian government.

In what appeared to be the final lifeline for the stricken aircraft pioneer, Fokker's court-appointed administrators said they, the Dutch state, engineer Stork and Deleye Investment signed a memorandum of understanding for a relaunch.

The administrators, who have run Fokker since it was declared bankrupt a year ago, said fresh negotiations would now begin with Khazanah, the Malaysian investment agency, to win its involvement in the relaunch.
All parties aimed to complete the plan by May 1, they said.

Under the deal, the Dutch and Malaysian governments, Stork and the investment vehicle owned by Andre Deleye, chairman of Dutch industrial group Begemann NV, would set up a new company to buy Fokker's aircraft-making assets.
Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers welcomed the move but warned against over-optimism.

"Breakthrough is a rather strong word, but it is a necessary step to see whether real breakthroughs can now be reached," he told Dutch television. "This (agreement) only involves the Dutch parties. If it stays that way, nothing will happen.

"Unless there's a good business plan that can convince all parties, then nothing will happen either, so there are a number of large and complex issues to be solved before we can get the idea that it's really heading the right way."

The various parties have been negotiating for weeks in an attempt to salvage something from the wreckage after majority shareholder Daimler Benz AG of Germany pulled the plug last March, saying it would no longer bear Fokker's huge losses.
Malaysia is Fokker's most likely eleventh-hour saviour after a number of potential suitors -- from Canadians and Koreans to Russians -- failed to come up with a viable rescue package.
Administrators have kept Fokker's factory near Amsterdam working on a handful of outstanding orders, but most of the company's skilled labour force has long since left.
The plant had been expected to close for good this summer and the assets liquidated.
